Utu brings a figure probably identifiable as Ninshubur from mountainous Šubur.

relations.myth: Prayer before the Cedar Forest expedition
relations.note: Ninsun petitions him to protect Gilgameš and challenges his responsibility for the hero's restlessness.

relations.myth: Ninsun’s prayer before the Cedar Forest expedition
relations.note: Ninsun petitions Šamaš to protect Gilgameš and asks Aya to remind him.
Ninurta gives Nisaba custody of agricultural abundance, grain heaps, and granaries.
Nusku leaves the Ekur to greet the returning divine warrior ceremonially.
Nusku announces and helps manage Ninurta's terrifying return to the divine court.
A first-millennium prayer calls Ninurta Nusku’s beloved brother.
Ninurta causes dikes or waters to overflow during Utnapishtim's flood.
Ninurta assigns Utu's judicial rites and powers to the favored hematite stone.
Learned traditions occasionally aligned Ninurta with Zababa while preserving their distinct cults.
Zababa is equated or compared with Ninurta and shares martial epithets, weapons, and court figures.
Nusku participates in negotiations and gift exchange involving Sud’s mother Nisaba.
Prayers to Nisaba and Tashmetu share a sequence through Nabû and learned culture.

relations.myth: Divine powers guard a patient from Lamaštu
relations.note: Nusku’s lamp and Pazuzu jointly protect the patient’s room.
Nusku’s lamp and Pazuzu’s head coexist as protective devices without a narrated alliance.
Pazuzu appears with seven demonic figures in the same apotropaic complex.
Offering lists and royal catalogues place Tašmetu with Zarpanitu’s household.
Tashmetu joined the Marduk–Ṣarpānītu circle and appeared with them in royal divine sequences.
relations.source: Sippar evidence and royal divine sequences

relations.note: Utu illuminates the boat; Ziusudra prostrates himself and sacrifices cattle and sheep.

Abarralaḫ.note: Abarralaḫ is listed among Enmesharra's seven sons.

Abu.note: Abu is one of eight deities produced to heal Enki.
Ninhursag generates Abu as one of Enki's eight healing deities.

Adamma.note: Adamma and Išḫara were co-invoked for deceased Eblaite kings.

Addu of Aleppo.note: Addu claims he fought Tiamat with weapons later granted to Zimri-Lim.

Admu.note: Nergal’s pairing with Admu could be transferred to syncretized Erra.
Cross-cultural learned theology lists the West Semitic Admu as Nergal's consort.

Aglibol.note: Aglibol shares residence and worship with Bel in Palmyra’s temple.

Agu.note: Agu and Išḫara were co-invoked for deceased Eblaite kings.

Alala.note: Alala follows Lahmu and Lahamu in the Anu-ancestry sequence.

Alammuš.note: Alammuš serves as Nanna’s vizier and household member.

Alla.note: Alla is Ningishzida's minister and presents a worshipper before him.
Variant manuscripts substitute Alla and Ningishzida as the disappearing young god.

Allani.note: Hurrian Allani and Akkadian Allatum became equated with Ereshkigal in theological transmission.
They jointly appear as underworld-associated goddesses during the crisis threatening Ebla.
Hurrian offering lists repeatedly place Išḫara near Allani.

Allatum.note: Šulgi-simti made offerings to Išḫara and Allatum at Puzrish-Dagan.

Ama-TUR-ma.note: The god list identifies Ama-TUR-ma as Ningishzida's sister.

Ama-abzu-E-kura.note: This deity stands at Hendursaga's behest for an assigned cosmic or civic task.

Ama-ušumgal-ana.note: An initially independent divine name was absorbed into Dumuzi’s identity.

Amar-Suen.note: Ur III royal theology includes Amar-Suen among Ninsun's sacral royal sons.

Amarra-azu.note: Amarra-azu is listed among Nanna’s children.

Amarra-he’ea.note: Amarra-he’ea is listed among Nanna’s children.

Amasagnudi.note: An Old Babylonian source reportedly equates or closely associates Amasagnudi with Ninshubur.
They appear among divine couples invoked together against Lamashtu.

Amurru.note: Some learned god lists equate Anu with Amurru despite their independent cult histories.
Some seals and lists make Geštinanna or Bēlet-ṣēri his consort.

An.note: An is plausibly reconstructed as Ezinan's sexual partner and the children's father.

An.myth: An deposits grain in the mountain
An.note: An brings Ezinan as divine grain from heaven and deposits her in a mountain.
A royal hymn assigns An as Geštinanna’s father.
Occasional theological language calls An Nanna’s father.
An acclaims Nanna in hymnic theology and may advise the exalted moon god.
An looks joyfully upon Nanshe as she occupies the divine dais.

An.myth: Establishment of Ninazu's throne and destiny
An.note: An establishes Ninazu's throne and determines a favorable destiny for him.
Lugalbanda imagines An bringing expert Ninkasi to provide beer service.
Later learned genealogies classify Ninsun among the daughters of An.

Annunītum.note: Annunītum and Išḫara received offerings in the same royal cult.

Annunītum.myth: Annunītum tramples Lamashtu and related afflictions
Annunītum.note: Medical-incantation material asks Annunītum to trample Lamashtu as an affliction.

Anuna gods.note: The Anuna create Grain and Sheep on the Holy Mound for divine consumption.
The Anuna acclaim Nanshe and participate in the destiny-deciding bird assembly.
The Anuna admire the divine temple-building work conducted within Nanshe’s sphere.
Keš is their dwelling, and Ninhursag belongs among the senior divine order.

Anunitu.note: The Anzû tradition calls Girra the son of Anunitu.

Anzud bird.note: Gilgamesh drives the Anzud bird from Inana’s occupied tree.

Arma.note: Sîn of Harran absorbed or displaced Arma’s lunar functions in eastern Anatolia.

Arsay.note: The standard list places Išḫara immediately after Arsay.

Aruru.note: Aruru leads Sud into Enlil's temple immediately before Sud receives the Ezina identity.
Aruru fashions Enkidu from clay as Gilgameš’s counterpart.
Aruru conducts Enlil’s bride Sud into Ekur and the marriage chamber.
At Anu’s command, Aruru creates Enkidu as Gilgamesh’s equal and check.
God lists coordinate Aruru with the same creator and mother-goddess complex.

Aruru.myth: Sud’s wedding procession into the Ekur
Aruru.note: Aruru escorts Sud into the Emah and Ekur and receives a household role.
The dossier describes Aruru as Ninlil’s sister-in-law within Enlil’s divine household.
God-list tradition coordinates Aruru with Ninmah's mother-goddess complex.

Asag.note: Learned lists group Anšar with Asag among superseded primordial powers.
Some learned and ritual traditions connect Asag’s origin with Anu.
Namtar and Asag jointly afflict sufferers and are expelled or transferred together.
Both are rejected as Enkidu’s killers; the netherworld itself seized him.
Asag's defeat occasions Ninurta's mountain gift and renaming of Ninhursag; they never fight directly.
Ninurta battles Asag and its hostile army of stones in the mountains.
Ninurta batters and uproots Asag, then celebrates over its body.
Ninurta renames or reclassifies the defeated Asag as Stone.

Asalluhi.note: Marduk absorbs Asalluhi’s exorcistic and magical identity.
Marduk absorbs Asalluhi's identity, exorcistic functions, and filial relationship to Ea.
His equation with Marduk transferred his spouse traditions to Zarpanitu.

Asalluḫi.note: Anšar confers Asalluḫi's name and identity upon Marduk.
Sumerian incantation tradition identifies Asalluḫi as Enki's son.
Nammu appears with Asalluḫi and Enki in the Eridu incantation circle.

Asari.note: Asari twice appeals to Enki about diseases brought by Namtar.

Ashtart.note: The standard list places Išḫara immediately before Ashtart.

Aya.myth: Ninsun’s prayer for the Cedar expedition
Aya.note: Aya participates indirectly when Ninsun petitions Šamaš and his wife.

Aya.myth: Prayer before the Cedar Forest expedition
Aya.note: Ninsun invokes Aya as an advocate for Gilgameš when Šamaš rests.
Aya/Šerida is Utu’s wife and intercedes favorably with him.
Aya prepares Šamaš’s evening meal when he enters his chamber.
Aya leads Nabû-apla-iddina into Šamaš’s presence during the restored cult.

Azimua.note: Azimua is one of eight deities produced to heal Enki.
Learned theology equates them because both are wives of Ningišzida.
Ninhursag generates Azimua as one of Enki's eight healing deities.

Ašgi.note: Ašgi is frequently treated as Ninhursag or Nintud's son at Keš.

Ašratum.note: Bēlet-ṣēri can function as a title of Ašratum or Gubarra.

Aštapinu.note: The Hurrian warrior god is explained as Zababa or Ninurta of Subartu.

Aššur.note: Royal inscriptions invoke Aššur and Adad together without a developed narrative encounter.
Assyrian theology identifies Anšar with Aššur, written AN.ŠÁR.
Assyrian theology transferred supreme political functions toward Aššur while retaining Anu’s senior rank.
Assyrian theology gives Aššur Marduk's authority over the divine assembly.
Assyrian theology calls Aššur the Enlil of the gods.
Assyrian theology assigns Aššur Enlil’s cosmic and royal status.
Neo-Assyrian theology places the Igigi beneath Aššur's universal authority.
Ishtar of Arbela and Nineveh jointly support Aššur’s chosen kings.
Aššur commands the good šēdu and lamassu to remain permanently in Sennacherib’s palace.
Assyrian adaptations substitute Aššur for Marduk in the Babylonian creation epic.
Assyrian theology interprets Marduk's ritual ordeal through Aššur's supremacy.
Sennacherib-era theology places Aššur upon Marduk’s serpent-dragon.
Assyrian theology invokes both gods to support royal authority and scholarship.
Sîn follows Aššur in invocations and supports Assyrian kingship.
Aššur and Nergal support imperial campaigns and deliver rebels to the king.
As Mullissu, Ninlil becomes Aššur’s wife after Assyrian theology gives him Enlil’s cosmic position.
Aššur and Mullissu jointly create, protect, legitimize, and enthrone Assyrian kings.
Nusku and Aššur jointly witness and enforce Assyrian loyalty oaths.
A possibly Aššur-associated winged disc appears above protective scenes.
Marduk’s Assyrian alignment with Aššur enabled Zarpanitu’s corresponding equation with Šerua.
Aššur and the Seven appear jointly in royal invocations and treaty lists.
Tashmetu was situated in Aššur’s temple environment, without a surviving narrative encounter.
The Assyrian recension assigns Marduk's role as Tiamat's opponent to Aššur.
Aššur receives the Babylonian champion's victory and titles through scribal substitution.
An Assyrian oracle declares Zababa the son of Aššur.

Aṣušu-namir.note: Ea's created emissary intervenes successfully before Ereshkigal and obtains life-restoring aid.
Ea creates and sends Aṣušu-namir to free Ishtar from below.

Baalshamin.note: Bel and Baalshamin held parallel civic sovereignty without a surviving narrative encounter.

Baba.note: Lagashite tradition identifies Baba as a daughter of An.
Cultic and list evidence places Ninsun near Baba in the Lagash pantheon.

Balīḫ.note: The deified river Balīḫ belongs to Aššur’s ceremonial court.

Bau.note: Gula claims Bau as her Lagaš manifestation in learned hymnic theology.
Bau’s Beneficent Lamma serves as her minister, intercessor, and guide.
Bau anoints the Eninnu bricks while Nanshe manages oracular messages.
A possibly displaced fragment mentions Bau bathing within the Nanshe C tradition.

Bau.myth: Marriage festival of Ningirsu and Bau
Bau.note: Ningishzida participates in the divine marriage celebration of Bau and Ningirsu.
Bau, wife of Ninĝirsu at Lagaš, became Ninurta's spouse through their identification.
Bau intercedes in prayer while Ninurta or Ninĝirsu renders judgment.
The canonical god list explicitly identifies Bau as Zababa’s wife.
Sennacherib fashioned their statues and established a joint Assyrian temple cult.

Belet-Terraban.note: Belet-Terraban and Išḫara received offerings in the same royal cult.

Belet-ili.note: The birth goddess helps create the humanity to which Atrahasis belongs.
The birth goddess preserves humanity under new reproductive limits after Atrahasis's survival.
Belet-ili laments the flood, swears remembrance, and excludes Enlil from Utnapishtim's sacrifice.

Belet-Šuḫnir.note: Belet-Šuḫnir and Išḫara received offerings in the same royal cult.

Belili.note: Akkadian and learned traditions describe Belili as Dumuzi’s sister or female mourner.
Learned tradition sometimes equates Belili with Dumuzi’s sister Geštinanna.
Some later learned traditions treat Belili as Geštinanna’s sister.
Some later learned traditions treat Belili as Geštinanna’s counterpart.
Belili follows Lahmu and Lahamu as Alala's feminine partner.

Belos.note: Damascius preserves Marduk as Belos, a demiurgic organizer of the cosmos.

Bilulu.myth: Bilulu blamed for Dumuzi’s desert death
Bilulu.note: A regional tradition blames Bilulu for his death, prompting Inanna’s vengeance.
Inanna kills or ritually transforms Bilulu after Dumuzi’s death.

Bilulu.myth: Bilulu receives a funerary ritual condition
Bilulu.note: Inanna assigns Bilulu a transformed fate associated with water skins and offerings.

Bilulu.myth: Bilulu becomes the desert protective goddess
Bilulu.note: Bilulu is transformed into a desert protective goddess functionally corresponding to the Lamma category.

Bison Bull.note: Lugal-e names the Bison Bull among Ninurta's previously defeated enemies.

Bull of Heaven.note: An controls the Bull at the horizon and relinquishes it to Inana.
Bull of Heaven.source: Gilgameš and the Bull of Heaven

Bull of Heaven.note: Enkidu grapples with and restrains the celestial Bull during its attack.
Enkidu helps Gilgameš kill the divine or divinely controlled Bull.
Gilgamesh and Enkidu battle the divine Bull released against Uruk.
Bull of Heaven.source: Sumerian Bull; Standard Babylonian Tablet VI

Bull of Heaven.note: Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill the Bull after it devastates Uruk.
Bull of Heaven.source: Sumerian Bull; Standard Babylonian Tablet VI

Bull of Heaven.myth: Ishtar unleashes the Bull upon Uruk
Bull of Heaven.note: Ishtar obtains, deploys, and later mourns the slain celestial Bull.
Šamaš receives the slain Bull of Heaven’s heart from Gilgameš and Enkidu.

Bunene.note: Some traditions identify the solar charioteer Bunene as Šamaš’s son.
Bunene serves as Šamaš’s minister and drives his solar chariot.

Buriyaš.note: Kassite lexical theology equates the weather god Buriyaš with Adad.

Bēl-āliya.note: Bēl-āliya receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.

Bēlet-balāṭi.note: This title can denote Gula, though at late Uruk it may name a distinct local goddess.

Bēlet-ilī.note: Bēlet-ilī fashions humans after the Anunnakū deliberate over the divine labor crisis.
Ea collaborates with Bēlet-ilī in creating humans from clay and a slain god.
One transferred Nergal genealogy makes Bēlet-ilī the mother of Erra.
The mother-goddess is invoked as an oath authority against Lamashtu.
Texts and royal inscriptions identify Bēlet-ilī with the Ninmah complex.
The Standard Babylonian Anzû epic identifies Bēlet-ilī as Ninurta's mother.
At Ea's urging, she commissions, blesses, and authorizes Ninurta to fight Anzû.

Bēlet-īli.note: Išḫara was apparently housed or worshipped in Bēlet-īli’s temple.

Bēlet-ṣēri.myth: Enkidu’s dream of the House of Dust
Bēlet-ṣēri.note: Bēlet-ṣēri kneels before Ereshkigal and reads the tablet of the dead.
Bēlet-ṣēri is the established Akkadian counterpart of Geštinanna.
The underworld scribe shares the Tablet XII setting with Gilgamesh.
Bēlet-ṣēri receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.

Cronus.note: Cronus warns Xisuthros in a dream and orders him to preserve writings and build a ship.

DINGIR.GE₆.note: DINGIR.GE₆ and Išḫara were grouped as related Ištar-type goddesses.

Dagan.note: Ugaritic and Syrian tradition makes the West Semitic storm god Dagan’s son.
Dagan announces or celebrates Anzu's defeat and the restoration of divine order.
Dagan.source: Standard Babylonian Epic of Anzu, Tablet III

Dagan.note: God lists and literary usage place Dagan in Enlil’s sovereign functional position.
Dagan authorizes or presides over Enmesharra's continuing confinement.
Dagan and Išḫara received offerings together without being identified as spouses.
Both deities occur together in Emar festival lists.
A damaged prayer places Dagan within the divine hierarchy surrounding Tashmetu’s passage.

Damgalnuna.note: Damgalnuna or Damkina is Enki's principal spouse and Marduk's mother.
Damgalnuna.source: Enūma eliš I and god lists

Damgalnuna.note: Damgalnuna is invoked with Ea to authorize Lamashtu’s expulsion.
She is conventionally reconstructed as Nanshe’s mother from Enki’s standard household.
Some traditions overlap Enki's spouse Damgalnuna with Ninhursag, though other sources distinguish them.

Damkina.note: Išḫara immediately follows Damkina in the treaty’s divine witness list.
Qingu and Damkina belong to the same Assur temple grouping.
Damkina bears Marduk and rejoices in his extraordinary form.
They appear among divine couples invoked together against Lamashtu.

Damu.note: Laments and god lists assimilate the two young disappearing gods despite their distinct origins.
Later theology makes Damu Gula's son through assimilation with Ninisina.
Gula is associated with rites mourning Damu's death or disappearance.
Later tradition presents Damu as Gula's co-healer.
Ninazu and Damu belong to the same group of lamented chthonic gods.
Damu.source: In the Desert in the Early Grass

Damu.note: Variant manuscripts substitute Damu for Ningishzida in corresponding lament positions.

Dari.note: Duri and Dari precede Lahmu and Lahamu in the Anu genealogy.

Dimpikug.note: Dimpikug and Namtar appear separately among the underworld recipients.

Dingirmah.note: Learned lists coordinate or equate Dingirmah with Ninmah and related goddesses.

Dingirmaḫ.note: Dingirmaḫ is a learned and cultic designation within Ninhursag's mother-goddess complex.

Dipar.note: The deified geographic power Dipar belongs to Aššur’s ceremonial court.

Dragon.note: Lugal-e names the Dragon among Ninurta's previously defeated enemies.

Duri.note: Duri and Dari precede Lahmu and Lahamu in the Anu genealogy.

Duttur.note: Duttur is Dumuzi’s mother in the pastoral genealogy.
She seeks or grieves for Dumuzi after anticipating his death.
Duttur is Dumuzi’s mother and therefore Geštinanna’s mother.
Mother and daughter appear together among Dumuzi’s mourners.
Ninsun overlaps with Duttur through limited traditions naming her as Dumuzi's mother.

Ea.note: Ea descends from Anšar through Anu.
Ea reports Tiamat's preparations and arranges Marduk's appearance before Anšar.
Ea belongs to the ancestral coalition and counsels within Aššur’s adapted creation narrative.
Ea appears as a member of Aššur’s ceremonial divine court.
A late divine address-book locates Išḫara within Ea’s temple.
Kingu is presented before Ea, executed, and his blood used for humanity.
As heir of Nudimmud, Nabu inherits Ea’s wisdom dynastically through Marduk.
The Amarna version addresses or treats Ea as Nergal's father.
Ea counsels and equips Nergal for his descent against Ereškigal.
Ea supplies disguise, strategy, and rules concerning gates and hospitality.
A parallel passage likewise credits Ea with granting and naming Zarpan.
Learned genealogy classifies Zarpanitu as Ea’s daughter-in-law through Marduk/Asalluhi.
Ea belongs to the divine lineage descending from Tiamat.
Ea is sent against Tiamat but withdraws because he cannot withstand her.
Ea kills Apsû, creating the conditions that eventually provoke Tiamat's rebellion.

Ea-šarru.note: Qingu is housed or worshipped in Ea-šarru's temple at Assur.

Eagle.note: Šamaš judges the eagle after it violates its oath and eats the serpent’s young.
Šamaš enables the eagle’s maiming by teaching the serpent a trap.
Šamaš arranges the guilty eagle’s restoration through Etana.

Earth.myth: Creation and arming of the Seven
Earth.note: Earth receives Anu’s seed and gives birth to the Seven.

Ebeh.note: The deified geographic power Ebeh belongs to Aššur’s ceremonial court.

Ebih.note: Inanna demands submission, attacks the deified mountain, and annihilates it.

Ebiḫ.note: Gibil's fire ravages Ebiḫ's forests, watercourses, and flanks.

Elagu.note: A Mesopotamian god list calls Elagu the Elamite Zarpanitu.

Elamatum.note: Girra kills Elamatum, who is subsequently installed in heaven.

Eleven monsters of Tiamat.note: Marduk defeats and binds the eleven monsters serving Tiamat.

Ememete.note: The canonical god list names Ememete as one of Ninkasi’s five children.

Enbilulu.note: Enlil fathers Enbilulu during disguised encounters with Ninlil.
Some god lists treat the irrigation deity Enbilulu as Enki's son.
Enlil fathers Enbilulu during his final disguised encounter with Ninlil.
Enbilulu is generated as Nanna’s brother in the underworld sequence.

Enbilulu.myth: Substitute sons for Suen in the underworld
Enbilulu.note: Ninazu and Enbilulu are brothers born as substitute underworld sons.
Ninlil conceives the irrigation god Enbilulu during Enlil’s ferryman disguise.

Enki and Ninki deities.note: The ancestral Enki-Ninki group perfects Ninlil’s powers throughout the lands.

Enki–Ninki deities.note: Learned god lists give Enlil long sequences of paired primeval ancestors.

Enmerkar.note: Enmerkar bears 'son of Utu' language expressing divine filiation or patronage.

Ennugi.note: One god-list tradition assigns Enmesharra as Ennugi's father.
The Igigi work within the hierarchy administered by the canal-controller Ennugi.
Ennugi and Ninkasi appear together among officials of Enlil’s divine household.
When Nanibgal is equated with Nisaba, Nisaba can inherit Nanibgal's marriage to Ennugi.
Ennugi and Nusku are grouped among the Ekur household gods.

Enoch.note: Scholars compare Enoch with Utuabzu and Enmeduranki through position, ascent, and revelation.

Enul.note: Enul is named as one of Nusku’s progenitors.

Enutila.note: Their separate defeats are juxtaposed without preserved direct interaction.
Enutila.source: Defeat of Enutila, Enmešarra, and Qingu

Enutila.note: Qingu and Enutila appear together in a fragmentary defeat tradition.
Enutila.source: Defeat of Enutila, Enmešarra, and Qingu

Enzi-kalama.note: A learned god list preserves Enzi-kalama as an additional consort-like figure.

Enšag.note: Enšag is one of eight deities produced to heal Enki.
Ninhursag generates Enšag as one of Enki's eight healing deities.

Eridu's fifty Anunna.note: A locally defined assembly of fifty Anunna is associated with Enki at Eridu.

Erragal.note: Later lists relate or equate Erragal with Erra, though their original identity remains disputed.
Erragal and the valiant Pleiades jointly accompany Marduk in battle.

Errakal.note: Errakal is sometimes equated with Nergal or Erra, but may remain independent.

Erua.note: Late theology makes Erua a name or pregnancy-associated aspect of Zarpanitu.

Etana.note: Šamaš directs childless Etana to the trapped eagle, enabling mutual aid.

Ezina.note: Nisaba establishes cultic offerings for Ezina.
The lament concludes by calling Nisaba Mother Ezina-Kusu.

Ešret-nabnīssu.note: Kingu receives offerings alongside this collective of Tiamat's creations.
Mummu and Ešret-nabnīssu jointly receive prescribed silver discs and offerings.

Fourteen helper gods.note: Ea's helper gods occupy Ereshkigal's gates during Nergal's armed invasion.

Fox.note: The fox negotiates with Enlil and brings Ninhursag back to heal Enki.

Ga-ga.note: Gaga reports Marduk's proposed kingship to the older gods.

Gaga.note: Gaga serves as Anšar's vizier and carries his summons and report.
Gaga bows before the pair and reports Tiamat's revolt and Marduk's terms.

Galla.note: The galla coerce her for Dumuzi’s location, but she remains silent.

Galla.myth: Galla surround Dumuzi at Geštinanna’s refuge
Galla.note: The galla locate Dumuzi with Geštinanna and surround him.

Gatumdug.note: Lagashite inscriptions call An the father of Gatumdug.
Ninsun has theological proximity to this maternal Lagash goddess without a narrated encounter.

Geme-Sîn.note: Sîn assists his pregnant divine cow through a difficult delivery.

Geštindudu.note: Geštindudu acts as Geštinanna’s adviser and female companion.

Girgire.note: Inanna kills or transforms Bilulu’s son while avenging Dumuzi.

Girgire.myth: Girgire receives a funerary ritual condition
Girgire.note: Inanna assigns Girgire a transformed ritual fate after Dumuzi’s death.

Gizzida.note: Gizzida responds favorably to mourning Adapa and intercedes at Anu’s gate.

Grain.note: Grain is created to provide food needed by the Anuna.
Grain.source: The Debate between Grain and Sheep

Gubbararae.note: Gubbararae is listed among Enmesharra's seven sons.

Gudam.note: Inanna confronts the destructive bull-like Gudam and determines his fate.

Gudanna.note: An astronomical commentary makes Kišar the spouse of Gudanna.

Gudea.note: Gudea is represented as Ninsun's divinely born royal son.

Gugalana.note: Ninazu is the Great Lord's seed; identification with Gugalana is probable.

Gugalanna.note: Gugalanna is named as Ereshkigal's deceased husband.

Guladu.note: Guladu and Išḫara were co-invoked for deceased Eblaite kings.

Gunura.note: Gunura becomes Gula's daughter through assimilation with Ninisina.
Gunura appears beside Gula in early records and later mourns Damu.
Gunura.source: Ur III administrative texts and laments

Gypsum.note: Lugal-e names Gypsum among Ninurta's previously defeated enemies.

Hadabal.note: Hadabal and Išḫara were co-invoked for deceased Eblaite kings.

Haia.note: Haia registers, enters, or deletes personnel on a tablet during Nanshe’s inspection.
In Sud’s regional genealogy, Haia fathers her through Nisaba.

Hanish.note: Hanish advances over hill and plain as a herald of the flood Utnapishtim survives.

Haya.note: Anšar is mentioned in Haya's hymn, but no narrative encounter is established.
Haya is Nisaba's standard spouse from the Old Babylonian period.
Nisaba handles tablets while Haya registers and deletes temple personnel.

Hayya.note: Ebla evidence probably equates Hayya with Ea, though the identification remains debated.

Hendursag.note: Hendursag examines testimony, distinguishes good from evil, and promulgates Nanshe’s decrees.

Hendursaĝa.note: Three heptads, including nocturnal animal-like warriors, serve under Hendursaĝa’s command.

Hittite Sun Goddess of the Earth.note: Anatolian adaptations use her as an equivalent of Ereshkigal or Allani.

Hutena-Hutellura.note: Išḫara immediately follows the birth and fate goddesses in the offering order.

Ibgirḫuš.note: Ibgirḫuš is listed among Enmesharra's seven sons.

Igalim.note: Originally Ningirsu and Bau’s son, Igalim was incorporated as a subordinate in Zababa’s court.
Igalim.source: Late Babylonian school and god lists

Iganakešda.note: A late god list assigns Iganakešda to a male Ninshubur configuration.

Igīgū.note: Nusku investigates the rebels’ grievance and relays their speeches to Enlil.

Ilaba.note: Scholars propose an uncertain equation after Sargon’s conquest of Kish.

Ilabrat.myth: Report of the broken South Wind
Ilabrat.note: Ilabrat identifies Adapa to Anu as Ea’s son and the breaker of the South Wind’s wing.
An Old Babylonian equivalence list identifies Ninshubur with the male minister Ilabrat.

Ilu-Bêti.note: A cow was offered first to Ilu-Bêti and then to Išḫara.

Inara.note: Hittite scribes sometimes used Sumerographic LAMMA for an Anatolian tutelary deity identified with Inara.

Irnina.note: An uncertain name formula may describe Lamashtu as seized by Irnina.

Ishtar of Babylon.note: The goddesses exchange hostile, jealous, or competitive words over Marduk.
Political theology partly assimilated her to Zarpanitu through the title Bēltiya.

Ishtar of Uruk.note: A proposed Babylonian policy incompletely aligned Uruk’s goddess with Bēltiya/Zarpanitu.

Isimud.note: Enki's vizier Isimud participates in the damaged narrative concerning Ezinan and her children.
The two-faced Isimud serves as Enki's minister, adviser, and messenger.
Enki orders Isimud to lead repeated efforts to recover the me from Inanna.

Isimud.myth: Isimud pursues the Boat of Heaven
Isimud.note: Enki’s minister repeatedly attempts to recover the me from Inanna.
Ninshubur repeatedly prevents Isimud from recovering Inanna’s boat and the me.
Ninurta raises his hand against Enki's messenger while pursuing greater control.

Ištar of Arbela.note: First-millennium theology associates or identifies Mullissu with Ištar of Arbela, while some royal texts distinguish them.

Ištar of Kiš.note: First-millennium lexical and theological tradition explicitly equates Ninlil with the goddess Ištar of Kiš.

Ištar of Nineveh.note: Mullissu converges with Ištar of Nineveh through shared residence and imagery, but remains distinct in some lists.

Ištar of Uruk.note: Erra devastates Uruk and its Ištar-associated dependants without a preserved direct encounter.

Ištar-Aššurītu.note: Tashmetu occupied an uncertain position within or near Ištar-Aššurītu’s cultic household.

Ištar-of-Babylon.note: Ištar-of-Babylon guards or holds Enmesharra's released sons at Ganṣir.
Ištar-of-Babylon.source: Defeat of Enutila, Enmešarra, and Qingu

Ištaran.note: Ištaran participates as a righteous lawsuit-decider when the gods establish standardized measures.
The Journey names both gods while variants redistribute their descending roles.

Išum.note: Išum mediates Erra's violence in a poem distinguishing the Anunnakū and Igīgū.

Išum.myth: Išum serves as Erra’s vanguard and interlocutor
Išum.note: Erra appoints Išum as his vanguard during the destructive campaign.

Išum.myth: Išum accompanies and channels Erra’s campaign
Išum.note: Išum accompanies Erra and redirects his violence toward restoring order.

Išum.myth: Išum persuades Erra to end his fury
Išum.note: Išum repeatedly rebukes Erra and ultimately calms his destructive rage.
Girra and Išum occur in the same fire-and-war poem without direct interaction.

Išum.myth: Erra's disruption of the cosmic order
Išum.note: Išum and the Igigi appear in the same cosmic drama without direct encounter.
Išum moderates Erra, allowing the order associated with Marduk to return.
Išum repeatedly counsels Erra against indiscriminate destruction.
Erra authorizes Išum's campaign, receives his report, and praises him.
Nergal and Išum jointly support the conquest of Thebes and campaigns against Elam.

Išum.myth: Alleged birth and abandonment of Išum
Išum.note: A damaged fragment may make Ninlil or Sud his mother, possibly through confusion with Sudaĝ.
Išum restrains and directs them, standing like a bolted door before them.

Kakka.myth: Messages between heaven and the underworld
Kakka.note: Kakka carries messages between Ereshkigal and the upper gods.
Ninshubur B identifies its divine speaker by both Ninshubur and Kakka.

Kalkal.note: Kalkal discovers the revolt and wakes Nusku.

Katunna.note: Learned lists possibly classify this minor deity as Zarpanitu’s child.

Ki.note: An and Ki form the primordial Heaven-and-Earth pair.
Their original unity is divided as the differentiated cosmos emerges.
Later schematic traditions make Enlil the offspring of heaven and earth.
Enlil separates Ki, earth, from An and orders the world.
Later cosmological genealogy treats Enlil as offspring of joined An and Ki.
Enlil separates heaven from Earth and establishes the cosmic axis.
A learned title may describe Nammu as mother of personified earth.
Learned cosmologies sometimes coordinate Ninhursag with the earth goddess Ki.

Kiki.note: Modern scholars propose that the Early Dynastic waterbird goddess merged with Nanshe.

Kippat-māti.note: Kippat-māti accompanies Tashmetu and Šērūa in an Assur temple procession.
Kippat-māti may have displaced Tashmetu in some Assur rituals under Sennacherib.

Kiririša.note: Modern scholarship compares or proposes an equation with Kiririša, but direct ancient evidence is absent.

Kitušgirizal.note: The canonical god list names Kitušgirizal as one of Ninkasi’s five children.

Kronos.note: Berossus equates Ea with the Greek god Kronos.

Kuli-ana.note: Lugal-e names Kuli-ana among Ninurta's previously defeated enemies.

Kumarbi.note: Ugaritic trilingual scholarship equates Hurrian Kumarbi with Enlil.

Kumarbi.myth: Invocation opening the Song of Kumarbi
Kumarbi.note: The singer invokes Išḫara among the gods summoned to hear Kumarbi’s tale.

Kura.myth: Ebla royal wedding and temple partnership
Kura.note: The royal couple offered to both, and Išḫara’s statue stood in Kura’s temple.
Kura embodied kingship while Išḫara protected the dynasty.

Kurgulgul.note: A Seleucid Uruk god list identifies Kurgulgul as Lugalbanda’s divine adviser.

Kurunnam.note: Kurunnam receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.

Kurunnītu.note: Two lamentation traditions identify the high-quality-beer deity Kurunnītu with Ninkasi.

Kusarikku.note: Lahmu and Kusarikku occur together in contest imagery and apotropaic ensembles.

Kusu.note: Kusu joins Ezinan in the compound Ezina-Kusu, possibly as epithet, association, or partial fusion.
Kusu and Ezina appear as distinguishable divine recipients of offerings.
Kusu appears with Ea in purification and statue-consecration rites.
Gibil appears within Kusu's liturgical network of purification deities.
Kusu receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.
Kusu and Ninkasi appear together among officials of Enlil’s divine household.
Nisaba establishes offerings intended to appease Kusu.
Kusu shares Nusku’s court grouping and appears with him in procession.

Kušuḫ.note: Išḫara and Kušuḫ jointly destroy the seed of oath-breakers.
The Hurrian moon god is contextually aligned with Sîn but sometimes listed separately.

Kūbu.note: Lamashtu is conjured by Kūbu beings whose authority coerces her.

Labar-TUR-ma.note: The god list identifies Labar-TUR-ma as Ningishzida's sister.

Lahar.myth: Creation and descent of Sheep and Grain
Lahar.note: Grain calls Sheep sister, and Enki orders them to remain together as sisters.
Sheep and Grain descend together and jointly bring prosperity, stores, and subsistence to humanity.
Grain disputes supremacy with Sheep and wins after Enki declares her greater.

Laṣ.note: Nergal’s marriage to Laṣ could be transferred to syncretized Erra.
Laṣ and Išum are jointly invoked among underworld-associated gods in a land-grant curse.
Offering lists and temple evidence pair Laṣ with Nergal at Kutha.

Lelwani.note: Late Hittite systematization sometimes places Lelwani in Ereshkigal's equivalence network.

Lilītu.note: A scholarly list equates a nighttime DIMME manifestation with Lilītu.

Lord Saman-ana.note: Lugal-e names Lord Saman-ana among Ninurta's previously defeated enemies.

Lugal-Maradda.note: Temple lists identify this local god of Marad as a form of Ninurta.

Lugal-irra.note: Lugal-irra and Išum are jointly invoked in the land-grant's curse section.

Lugal-ki-bura.note: His name occupies a role assigned to Ningishzida in other manuscripts.

Lugal-ki-suna.note: His name occupies a role assigned to Ningishzida in other manuscripts.

Lugal-šud-e.note: His name occupies a role assigned to Ningishzida in other manuscripts.

Lugaldukuga.note: Learned lists group Anšar with Lugaldukuga among superseded primordial powers.
Learned primeval genealogy places Lugaldukuga among Enlil’s ultimate ancestors.
Lugaldukuga receives offerings beside Enmesharra and stands near him genealogically.

Lugalhenŋal.note: A Seleucid Uruk god list identifies Lugalhenŋal as Lugalbanda’s divine secretary.

Lugalirra.note: Nergal-associated Meslamtaea and Lugalirra jointly guard entrances in first-millennium ritual.
Lugalirra functions as a divine doorkeeper in Nusku’s Nippur temple.

Lugalḫarrānu.note: A scholarly god list names Lugalḫarrānu as Ninsun's divine secretary or sukkal.

Lulal.note: The raised-fist divine guardian accompanies Pazuzu and Ugallu.

Luḫušû.note: This Nergal-like minor god is attached to Zababa’s late divine court.

Magilum Boat.note: Lugal-e names the supernatural Magilum Boat among Ninurta's defeated enemies.

Malik.note: Qingu and Malik belong to the same Assur temple grouping.

Mami.note: Mami is asked by Ea to command or inspire her son Ninurta against Anzu.
God-list theology pairs Erra with Mami as his wife.

Mami.myth: Creation of humanity after the labor revolt
Mami.note: The birth goddess creates humans with Ea to relieve the Igigi's labor.
Mami assumes Nammu's human-creator role in a separate Babylonian creation tradition.
Late theology calls Mami his mother, probably through Ninurta assimilation.
These Akkadian names alternate for the womb goddess identified with Ninhursag's wider complex.
Mami alternates with Nintu and Bēlet-ilī as the creator birth goddess.

Mammi.note: God lists assign Mammi or Mammitum as spouse of Nergal or Erra.

Mammitum.note: Mammitum and the Anunnaki jointly establish life, death, and human destinies.
Mammitum and Išum are jointly invoked in the land-grant's curse section.

Mamu.note: Mamu, the Sippar dream goddess, could be treated as Šamaš’s daughter.

Mandanu.note: A commentary maps Anšar's dispatch of Anu onto Mandanu's ritual journey.
Mandanu occupies a Babylonian warrior-partner role analogous to Ninurta.
Mandanu serves as a judge in Zababa’s expanded divine court.
Mandanu.source: Late Babylonian cultic and god lists

Manzat.note: One isolated Maqlû passage calls Manzat the sister of Šamaš.

Mardulaʾanki.note: Later interpretation of god lists identifies Mardulaʾanki as Namtar’s mother.
Mardulaʾanki.date: Old Babylonian to first millennium BCE

Medimša.note: Sumerian god-list tradition identifies Medimša as Iškur’s spouse.

Mekù.note: The canonical god list names Mekù as one of Ninkasi’s five children.

Meme.note: Meme's independent healing identity was substantially absorbed into Gula.

Meskilak.note: A proposed equation derives solely from the learned identification of their husbands.

Meslamta-ea.note: Meslamta-ea and Išum are jointly invoked in the land-grant's curse section.

Meslamtaea.note: Meslamtaea was assimilated to Nergal while also surviving as a distinct twin gate god.
Meslamtaea.source: Ur III records and god lists

Meslamtaea.note: Meslamtaea functions as a divine doorkeeper in Nusku’s Nippur temple.

Meḫuš.note: The canonical god list names Meḫuš as one of Ninkasi’s five children.

Mighty cow.note: A learned genealogical tradition makes the mighty cow Ninazu's mother.

Mullissu.note: Nusku and Mullissu jointly witness and enforce Assyrian loyalty oaths.

Mīšaru.note: Mīšaru is sometimes classified as Šamaš’s child, though other genealogies exist.
Personified Right Order belongs to Šamaš’s ritual and cultic entourage.

Nabarbi.note: A probable Išḫara figure stands beside Nabarbi according to reconstructed procession order.

Namma.note: Namma hears divine complaints, awakens Enki, and urges creation of human workers.
Namma initiates Enki's human-creation plan, over which Ninmah presides.
Namma kneads clay and gives form while Ninmah assists and determines work.

Nanaya.note: Late Urukian and god-list systems place Nanaya among Anu’s daughters or descendants.
Nanaya belongs to Ishtar’s circle and absorbs erotic and Urukean functions.
Babylonian tradition identifies Nanaya as Nabu’s beloved wife.
A ruler asks Nanaya to commend him favorably to her husband Nabu.
Offering lists and royal catalogues place Nanaya with Zarpanitu’s household.
Tashmetu and Nanaya appear as co-wife, rival, or complementary partners of Nabû.
Shared titles and transferred epithets produced partial, but never complete, identification.

Nanibgal.note: Some literary texts use Nanibgal as Nisaba's name, while most god lists distinguish them.

Narunde.note: Narunde is listed as sister of the Divine Seven of Elam.

Nazi.note: Nazi is one of eight deities produced to heal Enki.
Ninhursag generates Nazi as one of Enki's eight healing deities.

Neti.note: Neti reports Inanna's arrival and executes Ereshkigal's gate instructions.

Neti.myth: Neti strips Inanna at seven gates
Neti.note: The gatekeeper removes one item of Inanna’s regalia at each gate.

Nidaba.note: Particular regional genealogies identify Nidaba as An’s daughter.

Nimgir.note: Deified lightning Nimgir serves as Adad’s sukkal or minister.

Nin-MAR.KI.note: Some local traditions place Nin-MAR.KI as Nanshe’s daughter.

Nin-nigbunara.note: Nin-nigbunara stands at Hendursaga's behest for an assigned cosmic or civic task.

Ninagal.note: Nungalpiriggal constructs a bronze-and-lapis lyre according to Ninagal’s divine craft.

Ninazimua.note: Ninazimua and Namtar appear separately among the underworld recipients.
Ninazimua is Ningishzida's wife and receives funerary offerings beside him.

Ninbarag.note: Ninbarag assists or stands beside Nammu during humanity's birth.
Ninbarag assists Ninmah, though modern normalization of the name varies.

Ninbišukale.note: Ninbišukale stands at Hendursaga's behest for an assigned cosmic or civic task.

Nindara.note: Hendursaga serves Nindara as his accountant or administrator.
A damaged passage calls Nindara Hendursaga's older brother.
Nindara is her husband and the sea’s tax collector.

Ninegalla.note: The Lady of the Palace could be an Ishtar manifestation or distinct goddess.

Ningal.note: Ningal appears with Nanna as the Anuna bless the king and receive offerings.
The widespread later genealogy names Ningal as Inanna’s mother.
Protective goddesses receive offerings within temple service so Ningal accepts the king’s worship.
Lugalbanda names Ningal as Utu’s mother while praising the sun god.
Late texts occasionally merge Ningal with Ninlil or use Ninlil’s written name as Ningal’s epithet.
Harranian theology associates Ningal as the maternal figure in Nusku’s parentage.
Ningal, Nusku, Sîn, and Sadarnunna share residence and procession at Harran.
Ningal is Utu’s mother; Utu B calls him her son.

Ningirida.note: Ningirida is Ninazu's standard wife and approaches him in prayer.

Ningirim.note: Ningirim appears with Ea in purification and statue-consecration rites.

Ningirima.note: Ningirima precedes Nammu, who receives Ningirima's usual holy-water-basin title.

Ningirsu.note: Some early Lagashite material makes Ningirsu a son of An.
The Anuna marvel at or participate in the dedication of Ningirsu's temple.

Ningirsu.myth: Recovery of the Tablet of Destinies
Ningirsu.note: Ningirsu defeats Anzu and recovers the stolen Tablet in the early recension.
Anzu serves as Ningirsu's emblem, and Gudea compares Ningirsu's manifested form to Anzud.
Ningirsu.source: Early Dynastic art and Gudea inscriptions

Ningirsu.note: Ningirsu appears as Enlil’s child in a particular tradition.
Some local theology occasionally makes Ningirsu a child of Enki.
Ningirsu is her husband when Gula is identified with Bau at Lagaš.
Nanshe explicitly calls Ningirsu her brother while interpreting Gudea’s dream.
She identifies Ningirsu in Gudea’s dream and explains his temple-building command.
Their combined justice legitimates Gudea’s rule and protection of the vulnerable.

Ningirsu.myth: Construction and celebration of the Eninnu
Ningirsu.note: Ningishzida supports the construction and celebration of Ningirsu's Eninnu temple.
Lagash theology identifies Ninhursag as Ningirsu's mother.
Nisaba's star-tablet work translates Ningirsu's command into an architectural plan.
Their analogy enabled transfer of Bau, divine children, and weapons into Zababa’s circle.
Ningirsu.source: An = Anum V and school lists

Ningublaga.note: Ningublaga is listed as Nanna’s son and receives cult with him.

Ninguna.note: Ninguna assists or stands beside Nammu during humanity's birth.
Ninguna serves among Ninmah's assisting birth goddesses.

Ninigizibara.note: Ninigizibara is presented as Gula's healing identity or manifestation.

Ninimma.note: Ninimma receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.
Ninimma stands beside Nammu while she gives birth to humanity.
Ninimma and Ninkasi appear together among officials of Enlil’s divine household.
Ninimma serves among the birth goddesses assisting Ninmah during creation.
Some learned theological arrangements describe Ninimma as Ninurta's sister.
Conflicting learned arrangements call Ninimma Ninurta's lady or wife.
Ninimma and Nusku are grouped among the Ekur household gods.

Ninirigal.note: The learned god list assigns Ninirigal as Girra's wife.

Ninisina.note: Some healing-goddess genealogies define Ninisina as a daughter of Anu.
Ninisina is called Lady Gula and later translated or absorbed into Gula.
Ninisina enters before Enlil with kids and fruit in Ninlil’s sanctuary.
Healing-goddess and Pabilsaĝ equations brought Ninisina into a spouse relationship with Ninurta.

Ninkarrak.myth: Healing after the South Wind’s restoration
Ninkarrak.note: Ninkarrak heals disease associated with the restored South Wind, though no direct dialogue with Adapa survives.
Some learned healing-goddess genealogies call Ninkarrak a daughter of Anu.
Bilingual, lexical, and personal-name evidence treats Ninkarrak and Gula as equivalent in some contexts.
Ninkarrak.source: Bilingual texts and Kassite Nippur documents

Ninkarrak.note: The treaty invokes Išḫara beside Ninkarrak as an oath-enforcing deity.
Emar curse formulas pair them as divine punishers of oath-breaking.

Ninki.note: A primordial Ninki name-pair heads Enlil’s ancestral succession.

Ninkura.note: Ninkura’s divine craft perfects the forms of Sennacherib’s bull-colossus images.

Ninkurra.note: Ninkurra is Enki's daughter or granddaughter in the poem's successive genealogy.
Enki impregnates Ninkurra, described as his daughter or granddaughter.
Ninkurra is Ninhursag's granddaughter through Ninmu and Enki.

Ninkusi.note: A learned god list preserves Ninkusi as an additional consort-like figure.

Ninmada.myth: Mission to bring grain into Sumer
Ninmada.note: Ninmada joins the proposed mission to introduce Ezinan, the divine grain, into Sumer.
Ninmada assists or stands beside Nammu during humanity's birth.
Ninmada is explicitly addressed as Ninazu's brother.

Ninmada.myth: Proposed expedition for barley and flax
Ninmada.note: Ninazu invites Ninmada to obtain crops; Ninmada refuses without Enlil's command.
Ninmada and Ninkasi appear together among officials of Enlil’s divine household.
Andrew George suggests one learned configuration may treat Ninmada as Ninkasi’s daughter.
Ninmada assists Ninmah in the birth and creation scene.

Ninmena.note: God lists coordinate the royal birth goddess Ninmena with Ninhursag while sometimes distinguishing them.

Ninmešarra.note: Paired with Enmesharra as his spouse or female counterpart.

Ninmu.note: Ninhursag bears Ninmu after coupling with Enki.

Ninmug.note: Particular divine lists include Ninmug among Anu’s daughters.
Ninmug is securely attested as Išum's wife and intercedes with him.
Ninmug assists or stands beside Nammu during humanity's birth.
Ninmug serves among Ninmah's assisting birth goddesses.

Ninnibru.note: Late sources may use Lady of Nippur for Gula, though the identification remains ambiguous.
Nippur theology identifies Ninnibru as Ninurta's spouse.
Ninnibru receives the returning Ninurta and requests a blessing for the king.

Ninsianna.note: The personified planet Venus was assimilated to Inanna-Ishtar in later theology.

Ninsikila.note: The poem constructs the initially named Ninsikila as Ninhursag, without making the equation universal.

Ninsumun.note: Some genealogical texts call Gilgameš’s divine mother Ninsumun An’s daughter.
Learned genealogical tradition calls Nisaba and Ninsumun sisters.

Ninsutu.note: Ninsutu is one of eight deities produced to heal Enki.
Ninhursag generates Ninsutu as one of Enki's eight healing deities.

Ninti.note: Ninti is one of eight deities produced to heal Enki.
Ninhursag generates Ninti as one of Enki's eight healing deities.
The hymn names Ninti, queen of the abzu, as Ninkasi’s mother.

Nintinugga.note: Nippurian tradition functionally equates her with Gula while preserving her separate cult.
An incantation identifies the healing goddess Nintinugga as Ninazu's daughter.

Nintiḫal.note: The Nippur god list places Nintiḫal near Ninkasi in a beer-related cluster.

Nintu.note: Nintu and its variants function as names within Ninmah's goddess complex.

Nintud.note: The Keš birth goddess is frequently coordinated with Ninhursag but can be separately named.

Nintulla.note: Nintulla is one of eight deities produced to heal Enki.
Ninhursag generates Nintulla as one of Enki's eight healing deities.

Nintur.note: Ašnan and Nintur are invoked together against post-partum bleeding.
God lists secondarily associate Ninlil with Nintur-type mother-goddess figures.

Ninul.note: Ninul is named as one of Nusku’s progenitors.

Ninzaginna.note: Ninzaginna appears in the same compilation without direct exchange with Enmesharra.
Ninzaginna.source: Defeat of Enutila, Enmešarra, and Qingu

Ninĝirsu.note: Ninĝirsu and Geštinanna are grouped among deities favoring Gudea.
Local Ĝirsu warrior-agricultural god increasingly became identified with Ninurta.
Ninĝirsu.source: Explanatory god list and manuscript substitutions

Ninĝirzida.note: Ninĝirzida receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.

Ninšar.note: Ninšar and Ninkasi appear together among officials of Enlil’s divine household.
Ninšar and Nusku are grouped among the Ekur household gods.

Numušda.note: Some local traditions identify Numušda as Nanna’s son.

Nunbaršegunu.note: Nunbaršegunu is named as Ninlil’s mother; no father is given.
She warns Ninlil about bathing or walking by the canal and about Enlil’s intentions.

Nungal.note: Literary and list traditions can identify the prison goddess Nungal as An’s daughter.
The Nungal hymn tradition explicitly identifies Nungal as Ereshkigal's daughter.
The composition identifies its exalted goddess with Nungal in a local manifestation.

Nuska.note: Enlil orders his minister Nuska to ferry him to Ninlil.
Enlil sends Nuska as marriage envoy to Nisaba and Sud.
Particular texts call Nuska Enlil’s child, reflecting variable hierarchical kinship.
Girra and Nuska illuminate, protect, and avenge the ritual sufferer.
Later theology partly syncretized the two fire and light gods.
Nuska receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.
Nuska and Ninkasi occur together in a Nippur divine-court offering sequence.
Nuska transports Enlil by boat toward Ninlil before the river-bank encounter.
As Enlil’s envoy, Nuska brings the marriage proposal and lavish gifts to Sud’s mother.
Nuska brings Enlil's gifts and proposal to Nisaba after Sud's insult.

Nušiligga.note: The canonical god list names Nušiligga as one of Ninkasi’s five children.

Oannes.note: Adapa was later fused with Berossus’s amphibious culture-bringer through the learned Uanna-Adapa equation.

Other moon gods.note: Several regional oath lists place Išḫara alongside local lunar deities.

Pabilsag.note: Mother-goddess equations secondarily produce a genealogy in which Ninlil is Pabilsag’s mother.

Pabilsaĝ.note: He is Ninisina's beloved husband and later Gula's spouse at Isin.
Warrior theology and transferred spouse relations linked or equated Pabilsaĝ with Ninurta.

Palm-tree King.note: Lugal-e names the Palm-tree King among Ninurta's previously defeated enemies.

Papnunanki.note: Asalluhi’s spouse became a transferred name of Zarpanitu.

Papsukkal.note: Papsukkal serves Anu as chief minister and gatekeeper of Bīt Rēš.
Papsukkal is called the offspring of Enmesharra in a late prayer.
Later Akkadian theology assigns the male minister Papsukkal to Ishtar’s circle.
Later lists equate their offices and explain Ninshubur as Papsukkal regarding Anu.
Nusku takes position beside Papsukkal during the nocturnal procession.
Papsukkal serves Zababa as his vizier and divine attendant.

Patindu.note: Learned lists associate the libation deity Patindu with Ninkasi and Siraš.

Peštur.note: The Sumerian Bull composition calls Peštur Gilgamesh’s little sister.
Peštur.source: Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven

Pirinkir.note: Pirinkir and Išḫara were grouped as related Ištar-type goddesses.

Piriĝ-me.note: A Lagash royal inscription calls Piriĝ-me the child born by Ninsun.

Pleiades.note: Learned astral traditions contextually equate the Seven with the Pleiades.

Pēdu.note: The two underworld entrance officials jointly punish violators of a royal tomb.

Qingu.note: Anšar's faction opposes Qingu, Tiamat's commander, without a personal encounter.
Late lists classify Anšar and Qingu among defeated primordial beings.
Aššur defeats Qingu within the inherited rebellion and Tablet of Destinies plot.
Marduk identifies Qingu as the rebel leader responsible for revolt.
Marduk condemns Qingu to execution before humanity is made from his blood.
Ea kills or processes condemned Qingu and uses his blood to create humanity.
A scholarly god list or commentary explicitly equates Qingu with Enmesharra.
Qingu and Enmesharra are defeated within the same learned narrative complex.
Qingu.source: Defeat of Enutila, Enmešarra, and Qingu

Qingu.note: Mummu and Qingu are co-listed and receive parallel treatment as defeated primordial beings.
Tiamat takes Qingu as her second husband during preparations for war.

Qingu.myth: Qingu receives the Tablet of Destinies
Qingu.note: Tiamat enthrones Qingu and gives him the Tablet of Destinies and binding authority.
Tiamat appoints Qingu commander of her divine and monstrous battle force.

River.myth: Birth of the destructive Labbu dragon
River.note: River joins Sea in bringing forth the destructive monster.

Sadarnunna.note: Sadarnunna is Nusku’s regular wife in Nippur and Harranian cult.

Saggar.note: The Middle Assyrian recension assigns Saggar as Išḫara’s husband.

Sea.myth: Birth of the destructive Labbu dragon
Sea.note: Sea brings forth the monster; its personification and identification with Tiamat remain disputed.

Serpent.note: Šamaš teaches the serpent to trap the oath-breaking eagle in a bull carcass.

Seven attendants of Hendursaga.note: Seven subordinate heralds serve Hendursaga, patrol the land, and regulate dangerous or productive forces.

Seven-headed Snake.note: Lugal-e names the Seven-headed Snake among Ninurta's previously defeated enemies.

Sheep.note: Sheep is created to provide food and clothing needed by the Anuna.
Sheep.source: The Debate between Grain and Sheep

Shullat.note: Shullat advances over hill and plain as a herald of the flood Utnapishtim survives.

Shuruppak.note: The later recension names Ziusudra as Shuruppak's son.

Shuwala.note: Shuwala appears with Išḫara during Dagan’s kissu festival.

Siduri.note: Siduri counsels Gilgamesh during his search for the immortal flood survivor.
Siduri.source: Old Babylonian Sippar; Standard Tablet X

Simut.note: Mesopotamian lexical theology connects the Elamite Simut with Nergal through martial and Martian associations.

Siraš.note: Siraš receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.
The canonical god list equates Ninkasi with the beer goddess Siraš.
A Neo-Assyrian bilingual recension renders Sumerian Ninkasi as Akkadian Siraš.
An Assur recension treats Ninkasi and Siraš as sisters rather than identical.

Siris.note: A late or isolated learned tradition makes Anzu a child of Siris.

Six-headed Wild Ram.note: Lugal-e names the Six-headed Wild Ram among Ninurta's defeated enemies.

Sol.note: Roman interpretation could translate or equate local Šamaš with Sol.

Solar deity.note: Zababa is dispatched because the solar deity disappeared, but no meeting survives.

South Wind.note: The South Wind overturns Adapa’s boat; his effective curse breaks its wing and stops it for seven days.

South Wind.myth: Adapa breaks the South Wind’s wing
South Wind.note: Adapa curses and breaks the South Wind’s wing after it overturns his boat.
Adapa breaks the South Wind's wing using power granted by Ea.

Strong Copper.note: Lugal-e names Strong Copper among Ninurta's previously defeated enemies.

Sud.note: After marrying Enlil, Sud is explicitly renamed or reclassified as Ezina.
Enlil propositions and insults Sud, who sharply rebukes him.
Enlil formally seeks Sud’s hand and marries her after sending gifts.
After marrying Enlil and entering Ekur, Sud receives the name Ninlil.
The regional goddess Sud becomes identified with Ninlil through marriage and renaming.

Sudaĝ.note: Some scholars reconstruct Sudaĝ or Aya as his mother from related traditions.

Suhurmāšu.note: A goat-fish associated with Ea is engraved on a Pazuzu amulet.

Tarḫunt.note: Hittite and Luwian writing equates Anatolian Tarḫunt with Adad through the IM logogram.

Tašme-zikru.note: The god list assigns Tašme-zikru as Išḫara’s female vizier or attendant.

Teššub.note: Multilingual scribal culture translates or equates the Hurrian weather god Teššub with Adad.
Išḫara intercedes for Ebla when Teššub threatens its destruction over refused emancipation.
Išḫara appears in sacrificial series belonging to Teššub and Ḫepat.

Tiamat's eleven creatures.note: Kingu commands Tiamat's collective host of eleven dangerous creature types.

Tišpak.note: Marduk appropriates the mušḫuššu formerly associated with Tišpak.
Išḫara and Tišpak jointly witness an Old Babylonian diplomatic oath.
Marduk acquires the mušḫuššu, which was previously associated with Tišpak.
Tišpak rides or stands upon the serpent-dragon as his controlled animal.
Tišpak kills the giant lion-serpent and wins kingship; identification as mušḫuššu is disputed.
Tišpak partially assimilates Ninazu and inherits his Ešnunna office and temple.

Tišpak.myth: Ambiguous stewardship or barrier against Tiamat
Tišpak.note: Tišpak is called her steward, administrator, or possibly a barrier against her waters.

Turtle.note: Enki's supernatural turtle digs a covered pit and defeats or traps Ninurta.
The deliberately created turtle humiliates Ninurta for his post-victory overreach.

Tutu.note: Borsippa’s Tutu becomes a name or aspect of Marduk.
Marduk absorbs Tutu through learned theological equations and name explanations.

Uanna.note: Late learned texts combine Uanna with Adapa, though Adapa may function there as an epithet meaning wise.

Ubara-Tutu.note: Utnapishtim is Ubar-Tutu's son; Berossus preserves the ancestry through Otiartes.
W-B 62 places an apparent Shuruppak generation between Ubara-Tutu and Ziusudra.

Ugallu.note: The armed lion-headed guardian appears beside Pazuzu in protective assemblages.

Ugur.note: Ugur appears with Išḫara during Dagan’s kissu festival.
Lexical and god-list traditions describe Ugur as Nergal's weapon or attendant.

Ugurtu.note: Qingu and Ugurtu belong to the same Assur temple grouping.

Ukulla.note: Tišpak's spouse occasionally occupies Ninazu's consort position through local rearrangement.

Ulmašītum.note: Ulmašītum and Išḫara received offerings in the same royal cult.

Ulāya.note: The deified river Ulāya belongs to Aššur’s ceremonial court.

Umul.note: Ninmah cannot feed, address, or assign a sustainable fate to Enki's creation.

Ungasaga.note: The god list assigns Ungasaga to Nisaba as a sukkal attendant.

Untamable bull.note: A learned genealogical tradition makes the untamable bull Ninazu's father.

Ur-Namma.note: Ur-Namma and his dynasty were incorporated into the Ninsumuna–Lugalbanda ancestral family.
Ur-Namma.source: Ur III hymnic and administrative texts

Ur-Namma.note: Royal hymns identify Ninsun as the divine mother who gave Ur-Namma birth.
Ur-Namma builds the Emaḫ temple for Ninsun as his personal goddess.

Ur-šanabi.note: Ur-šanabi ferries Gilgamesh across the Waters of Death to Uta-napišti.

Uraš.note: One isolated Old Babylonian prayer names Uraš as Iškur’s mother.
Third-millennium regional traditions pair heavenly An with the earth goddess Uraš.
A royal hymn assigns Uraš as Geštinanna’s mother.
Uraš is Ninisina's mother; the genealogy transfers to Gula through identification.
Uraš occupies Nammu's spouse-of-An and mother-of-Enki positions in an alternative genealogy.
A late learned genealogy lists Uraš as Ninshubur’s parent.
Uraš is sometimes inferred as Ninsun's mother where she is paired with An.
Nisaba is called the great wild cow born by Uraš.

Uraš of Dilbat.note: First-millennium genealogy presents the male tutelary god Uraš as Tashmetu’s father.

Urbadda.note: Urbadda is listed among Enmesharra's seven sons.

Urbadḫumḫum.note: Urbadḫumḫum is listed among Enmesharra's seven sons.

Urmašum.note: Urmašum is listed among Gula's sukkals or attendants.

Urumaš.note: Urumaš dwells as herald of the plain in Ninhursag's temple household.

Uršabiduga.note: Uršabiduga is listed among Gula's sukkals or attendants.

Uta-napišti.note: Ea warns Uta-napišti through a reed wall, enabling his survival.
Šamaš supplies the appointed weather signal for Uta-napišti to board his vessel.

Utnapishtim’s wife.note: Enlil grants Utnapishtim’s wife immortal life with her husband.

Uttu.note: Uttu's weaving is juxtaposed with Sheep and Grain in the debate's cosmogonic opening.
Uttu descends from Enki through the poem's succession of divine births.
Enki pursues and impregnates Uttu before Ninhursag removes his semen.
Uttu is Ninhursag's great-granddaughter in the poem's generational sequence.
Ninhursag advises Uttu how to deal with Enki.
Ninhursag removes Enki's semen from Uttu's body and grows eight plants.

Utuabzu.note: Adapa’s heavenly journey resembles Utuabzu’s ascent, prompting later conflation despite no secure identity.

Ušmu.note: Nusku and Ušmu jointly take positions beside Papsukkal.

Ušumgallu dragon.note: Lu-Nanna drives an ušumgallu dragon from E-ninkarnunna.

We-ilu.note: As Mami, she mixes We-ilu's flesh and blood with clay to form humanity.

Weather god.myth: Search for the missing solar deity
Weather god.note: The weather god dispatches Zababa to seek the absent solar deity.

Wer.note: Lexical theology equates the north Babylonian or Syrian weather god Wer with Adad.

Winter.note: Winter produces abundant grain and makes Ezina appear radiant in the furrows.

Wurunkatte.note: Hittite texts render or compare this Anatolian war god through Zababa logograms.

Wê.myth: Creation from divine blood and clay
Wê.note: Wê is slain so his flesh and blood can be used to create humanity.

Wê-ila.myth: Slaying of the god used to create humanity
Wê-ila.note: His flesh and blood create humans who inherit the Igigi's former work.

Wê-ilu.note: Ea proposes creating humanity using clay and the slain god's flesh and blood.

Wê-ilu.myth: Creation from divine flesh and blood
Wê-ilu.note: The birth goddess mixes his flesh and blood with clay to form humanity.

Yarhibol.note: Yarhibol shares residence and worship with Bel in Palmyra’s temple.

Zamaḫḫunde.note: Zamaḫḫunde is listed as jester or attendant of the Divine Seven of Elam.

Zisummu.note: Zisummu is listed among Enmesharra's seven sons.

[Na]mtartu.note: A damaged restoration possibly names her as Namtar’s female counterpart.
[Na]mtartu.source: Underworld Vision of an Assyrian Prince

all the gods.note: Nammu is called the primeval mother who gave birth to all gods.

bašmu.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the bašmu as part of her battle force.

divine assembly.note: The divine assembly expels Enlil from the city as ritually impure.

foreign gods.note: Captured foreign gods are subordinated, transported, restored, or returned under Aššur’s sovereignty.

fox.note: A fox helps restore communication between the afflicted Enki and Ninhursag.

gala-tura and kur-ĝara.note: After they echo her cries, Ereshkigal grants them Inanna's hanging corpse.

galatur.note: Enki fashions the galatur and equips it to help restore Inanna.
Enki’s created emissary helps obtain and revive Inanna’s corpse.

galla.note: Utu’s transformations temporarily frustrate the demons pursuing Dumuzid.

girtablullû.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the girtablullû as part of her battle force.

junior gods.note: Enlil directs their labor and confronts their revolt against its burden.

kulullû.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the kulullû as part of her battle force.

kurgarra.note: Enki fashions the kurgarra and equips it to help restore Inanna.
Enki’s created emissary helps obtain and revive Inanna’s corpse.

kusarikku.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the kusarikku as part of her battle force.

lillû.note: Some King List manuscripts name a lillû as Gilgamesh’s father.

mušmaḫḫu.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the mušmaḫḫu as part of her battle force.

scorpion-beings.myth: Passage through the mountains of Māšu
scorpion-beings.note: Gilgamesh encounters the scorpion-beings while seeking the road beyond Māšu.

seven sons.note: The epic calls Humbaba’s personified supernatural defenses his seven sons.

snake.note: A snake steals Gilgamesh’s plant while he bathes and sheds its skin.

the Anunna.note: Ninshubur appeases the Anunna and provides their offerings.

the Anunna judges.note: The netherworld judges pronounce judgment against Inanna.

the Sebitti.note: The Sebitti receive cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.

the evil lilû-demons.note: Pazuzu proclaims himself king of the evil lilû-demons.

the galla.myth: Galla pursue Dumuzi as Inanna’s substitute
the galla.note: The netherworld demons chase, bind, and seize Dumuzi after Inanna surrenders him.

the galla.myth: Galla capture and kill the fugitive shepherd
the galla.note: Despite repeated escapes and transformations, the demons beat, bind, and kill or drag Dumuzi below.

the galla.myth: Galla torture Geštinanna and find Dumuzi
the galla.note: The demons hunt Dumuzi, torture his sister, and eventually find him at the sheepfold.
The galla accompany the restored goddess and seize Dumuzi in her place.

the seven Anuna judges.note: They sit with Ereshkigal, condemn Inanna, and enforce the substitute requirement.

the seven children.myth: Ezinan gives birth to seven children
the seven children.note: Ezinan bears seven unnamed children; the youngest suffers impairment or abandonment.

the winds.myth: The mountain and the broken wings
the winds.note: Pazuzu travels among the winds and breaks their wings individually.

the younger gods.note: Mummu urges Apsû to suppress or destroy the noisy younger divine generation.

turtle.note: Enki fashions a turtle from Abzu clay to seize Ninurta.

ugallu.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the ugallu as part of her battle force.

urīdimmu.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the urīdimmu as part of her battle force.

ušumgallu.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the ušumgallu as part of her battle force.

Ĝatumdug.note: The composition maps the exalted healing goddess onto Ĝatumdug in her local city.
Ĝatumdug supplies her favorable lamma to accompany and protect Gudea.
Nanshe and Ĝatumdug jointly found and protect Lagash in local theology.
Ĝatumdug ritually births temple bricks while Nanshe oversees oracular decisions.

Ĝirĝire.note: Bilulu’s son is implicated in Dumuzi’s death and consequently punished by Inanna.

Ĝirĝire.myth: Ĝirĝire becomes the desert protective god
Ĝirĝire.note: Ĝirĝire is transformed into a desert protective god corresponding functionally to the Alad category.

ŠAR.ŠAR.GABA.note: This uncertainly read goddess assists Nammu during humanity's creation.

Šakkan.note: Grain identifies Šakkan as Sheep's herdsman while belittling her rival.

Šakkan.myth: Creation and arming of the Seven
Šakkan.note: They are commissioned to destroy livestock protected by Šakkan.

Šala.note: Šala is Adad’s regular Akkadian spouse and fertility partner.
Adad and Šala receive joint cult and jointly threaten tablet thieves.
Šala.source: Late Babylonian and Seleucid ritual texts

Šalaš.note: Šalaš is named as Girra's mother.

Šamaš.note: Šamaš and Adad jointly reveal divine decisions through extispicy.
Šamaš and Adad are consulted about whether Zababa is Aššur’s son.
Royal inscriptions invoke Šamaš beside Aššur.
Šamaš exposes ritual evil while Ea provides purification in their joint invocations.
Šamaš receives the luminous splendour confiscated from Enmesharra.

Šamaš.myth: Erra’s disorder affects justice and cosmic light
Šamaš.note: Erra’s violence disrupts Šamaš’s spheres, though no secure direct dialogue survives.
The Igigi belong to the divine assembly before which Šamaš exercises judgment.
Šamaš's statue joins Marduk's restoration procession.
Šamaš’s symbol shares legal-symbolic registers with the mušḫuššu.
Nergal and Šamaš jointly validate kingship, justice, or military action.
A royal prayer calls Nusku the friend and companion of Šamaš.
Maqlû transfers a daytime Šamaš judicial formula to Nusku for nocturnal use.
Šamaš’s solar symbol appears above the Pazuzu-protected scene.
Šamaš is diverted while the Seven attack and obscure Sîn.
Šamaš and Adad jointly declare that Zababa is Aššur’s son.

Šamḫat.note: Šamḫat has intercourse with Enkidu, separating him from the animals.
Šamḫat clothes Enkidu and introduces him to human food and society.

Šar-ṣarbati.note: Šar-ṣarbati is jointly listed with Išum, Nergal, and Šubula.

Šara.note: Some Sumerian literary or god-list traditions call Šara a son of An.

Šara.myth: Divine assembly after the Tablet theft
Šara.note: Šara is summoned as a possible champion against Anzu but refuses.
Šara is asked to fight Anzû but declines or proves unequal.
Šara and Girra appear among the divine candidates refusing the Anzû mission.
Šara refuses to confront Anzû before Ninurta accepts the commission.

Šargaz.note: The deified weapon Šargaz appears among the figures serving Zababa’s court.

Šarur.myth: Battle for the Tablet of Destinies
Šarur.note: Ninurta's sentient weapon carries tactical counsel and participates in the campaign against Anzu.
His animate mace scouts, warns, embraces, counsels, and carries messages during battle.
Šarur carries instructions between Ninurta and Enlil.
Ninurta’s deified speaking weapon was attached to Zababa’s court without a surviving adventure.

Šassūrātu.note: The womb goddesses receive Mami's clay portions and gestate the first humans.

Šauška.note: The Hurrian goddess Šauška was equated with Ishtar while retaining distinct traditions.
Scribal usage partially assimilated them, although explicit lists could distinguish them.

Šenbarimime.note: Šenbarimime is listed among Enmesharra's seven sons.

Šerua.note: Mullissu overlaps or converges with Šerua as Aššur’s spouse, though sources do not always fully equate them.
Assyrian theology equated Zarpanitu with Šerua by spousal analogy and phonetic resemblance.

Šeruʾa.note: Some Neo-Assyrian theological classifications present Šeruʾa as Aššur’s wife.
Other Neo-Assyrian classifications instead present Šeruʾa as Aššur’s daughter.

Šilamkurra.note: A learned god list heads Lugalbanda and Ninsun’s group of minor divine children with Šilamkurra.
Modern reconstructions of An = Anum include Šilamkurra among her children.

Šimige.note: Hurrian Šimige was equated with Šamaš in bilingual and scribal practice.

Širuḫi.note: The trilingual list places Ninazu and Hurrian Širuḫi in equivalent columns.

Šu-Suen.note: A royal hymn explicitly calls Šu-Suen the son of Ninsun.

Šubula.note: A damaged god-list passage possibly makes Šubula his son; Nergal is an alternative father.
Išum and Šubula are repeatedly paired in underworld, offering, and river-god contexts.

Šulgi.note: The deified king Šulgi styles himself Geštinanna’s son.
Royal hymnology represents the deified Šulgi as Geštinanna’s brother.
Šulgi dedicates gold earrings to Geštinanna.
Šulgi presents Lugalbanda as his divine father in royal kinship theology.
Ninsun is Šulgi's true divine mother, cherishing him from the womb.
The deified king dedicates an anthropomorphic statue to Ninsun of Ur.

Šulinkatte.note: Hittite texts render or compare this Anatolian war god through Zababa logograms.

Šullat.note: Šullat advances before or beside Adad as the deluge begins.

Šulpae.note: God lists and local traditions pair Šulpae with Ninhursag.
God-list theology assigns Šulpae as spouse of the mother goddess.

Šulpaea.note: Erra threatens to dim Šulpaea’s brilliance in celestial-divinatory language.

Šulšagana.note: Šulšagana was transferred from Ningirsu’s circle into Zababa’s expanded court.
Šulšagana.source: Late Babylonian school and god lists

Šumaḫ.note: Some Ninisina genealogies include Šumaḫ as her child, indirectly transferring the relationship to Gula.

Šuzianna.note: A learned god list preserves Šuzianna as an additional consort-like figure.
Šuzianna is explicitly called Enmesharra's daughter in one tradition.
Šuzianna receives cultic accommodation in or association with Gula's late Nippur temple.
Šuzianna assists or stands beside Nammu during humanity's birth.
Šuzianna and Ninkasi occur together in a Nippur divine-court offering sequence.
Šuzianna assists Ninmah and Namma in the human-creation process.
Šuzianna is co-worshipped in Nusku’s Nippur temple.

Šērūa.note: The king escorts Šērūa, Kippat-māti, and Tashmetu together into Anu’s temple.

ūmū dabrūtu.note: Tiamat fashions and arms the fierce storm demons as part of her battle force.

ᵈUR.note: This deity is equated with Urmašum and listed in Gula's court.

Ḫabūrītum.note: Both received distinct offerings in the same royal archive.

Ḫala.note: Kassite lexical scholarship glosses the poorly known goddess Ḫala as Gula.

Ḫamun-ana.note: The god list assigns Ḫamun-ana to Nisaba as a sukkal attendant.

Ḫanbu.note: Pazuzu repeatedly identifies himself as the son of Ḫanbu.

Ḫaniš.note: Ḫaniš accompanies Šullat and Adad during the flood assault.

Ḫaštamer.note: The Middle Assyrian recension assigns Ḫaštamer as Išḫara’s son.

Ḫaḫḫima.note: The frost being freezes or immobilizes Zababa during his unsuccessful mission.

Ḫedimmeku.note: God lists call her Namtar’s daughter, despite a conflicting genealogy under Enki.
Ḫedimmeku.date: Later second to first millennium BCE

Ḫendursaga.note: Old Babylonian scholars equated the originally distinct Akkadian and Sumerian gods.

Ḫepat.note: Išḫara belongs to Ḫepat’s ordered offering circle.

Ḫešui.note: Zababa’s logographic writing designates the Hurrian war god Ḫešui in some contexts.

Ḫišamītum.note: A bird omen names a single divinatory position belonging to both goddesses.

Ḫušbišag.note: She is Namtar’s wife and shares his underworld court status.

Ṣilluš-ṭāb.note: Learned lists possibly classify this minor deity as Zarpanitu’s child.
